chunks.heading: Metal atoms share their electrons
chunks.body: In a metal, outer electrons break free and drift through the whole structure as a 'sea' of delocalised electrons. This sea attracts the positive metal ions, holding the metal together.
chunks.checkText: In the metallic bonding model, delocalised electrons are...

checkOptions.text: Free to move through the whole metal

chunks.heading: Why metals conduct electricity
chunks.body: Metals conduct electricity because their [[chem-metallic-bonding-model|delocalised electrons]] are free to move. When a current is applied, these electrons flow through the metal.
chunks.checkText: Metals conduct electricity well because they contain...

chunks.heading: Why metals bend instead of breaking
chunks.body: When a force pushes on a metal, layers of positive ions can slide past each other. The [[chem-metallic-bonding-model|sea of electrons]] moves with them, so the metal bends instead of shattering.
chunks.checkText: Metals are malleable (bendable) because...

checkOptions.text: Layers of ions can slide while the electron sea holds them together
The ions are not attracted to each other

chunks.heading: Metal meets non-metal: electrons transfer
chunks.body: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, the metal atom transfers its [[chem-valence-electrons|valence electrons]] to the non-metal atom. The metal becomes a positive ion and the non-metal becomes a negative ion.
chunks.checkText: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, the metal atom...

checkOptions.text: Loses electrons to become a positive ion

chunks.heading: Ions pack into a lattice
chunks.body: Positive and negative ions arrange into a huge three-dimensional lattice, held together by electrostatic attraction called ionic bonding. This attraction is very strong, giving ionic solids very high melting points.
chunks.checkText: Ionic bonding is the...

checkOptions.text: Electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions
Sharing of electrons between two atoms
Sea of electrons around metal ions

chunks.heading: Why ionic solids shatter
chunks.body: A hard knock can shift a layer of ions in the [[chem-ionic-lattice|lattice]], lining up ions with the same charge. These like charges repel, so the crystal shatters instead of bending.
chunks.checkText: Ionic crystals are brittle because a hard knock can...

checkOptions.text: Line up same-charge ions next to each other, causing repulsion
Make the ions attract more strongly

chunks.heading: When ionic compounds conduct electricity
chunks.body: In a solid, ions are locked in the [[chem-ionic-lattice|lattice]] and can't move, so it doesn't conduct electricity. Once melted or dissolved in water, the ions become free to move and conduct.
chunks.checkText: A solid ionic compound does not conduct electricity because its ions...

chunks.heading: Sharing instead of transferring
chunks.body: When two non-metal atoms bond, they share a pair of [[chem-valence-electrons|valence electrons]] instead of transferring them. This sharing is called a covalent bond.
chunks.checkText: A covalent bond forms when two atoms...

chunks.heading: Single, double and triple bonds
chunks.body: A single bond shares one pair of electrons, a double bond shares two pairs, and a triple bond shares three pairs. More shared pairs make a stronger bond.
chunks.checkText: A triple covalent bond involves how many shared pairs of electrons?

chunks.heading: Drawing electrons as dots
chunks.body: A Lewis dot diagram shows an atom's [[chem-valence-electrons|valence electrons]] as dots. Dots between two atoms are a shared bonding pair; dots left on one atom are a non-bonding lone pair.
chunks.checkText: In a Lewis dot diagram, a pair of dots between two atoms represents...

checkOptions.text: A shared bonding pair of electrons

chunks.heading: Bonds inside vs forces between
chunks.body: The [[chem-covalent-bond|covalent bonds]] inside a molecule are strong and are called intramolecular bonds. The forces holding separate molecules together are much weaker and are called intermolecular forces.
chunks.checkText: Which are generally weaker: intramolecular bonds or intermolecular forces?

chunks.heading: Electron pairs push each other apart
chunks.body: Electron pairs around an atom repel each other and spread out as far apart as possible. This is why methane's four bonding pairs form a tetrahedral shape.
chunks.checkText: According to VSEPR theory, electron pairs around an atom arrange themselves to be...

checkOptions.text: As far apart from each other as possible

chunks.heading: When sharing isn't equal
chunks.body: If two bonded atoms have different [[chem-electronegativity|electronegativity]], the more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer. This unequal sharing gives the bond a small positive and negative end, called a dipole.
chunks.checkText: A polar covalent bond forms when the atoms in the bond have...

chunks.heading: Does the whole molecule end up polar?
chunks.body: A molecule is polar only if its [[chem-polar-covalent-bond|polar bonds]] don't cancel out. Symmetrical molecules cancel their bond dipoles and are non-polar; asymmetrical molecules stay polar.
chunks.checkText: A molecule with polar bonds arranged symmetrically will be...

chunks.heading: The weakest force, found everywhere
chunks.body: Electrons moving randomly can briefly bunch up on one side of a molecule, creating a temporary dipole. This flickering attraction between molecules is called a dispersion force, and it exists between all molecules.
chunks.checkText: Dispersion forces are present...

checkOptions.text: Between all molecules, polar or non-polar

chunks.heading: Polar molecules attract each other
chunks.body: In [[chem-molecular-polarity|polar molecules]], the positive end of one molecule is attracted to the negative end of another. This is called a dipole-dipole force, and it's stronger than a dispersion force.
chunks.checkText: Dipole-dipole forces occur between...

chunks.heading: An extra-strong attraction
chunks.body: When hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, the resulting [[chem-dipole-dipole-forces|dipole-dipole force]] between molecules becomes especially strong. This hydrogen bonding is why ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.
chunks.checkText: Hydrogen bonding happens when hydrogen is bonded to...

chunks.heading: One giant molecule
chunks.body: Some substances, like diamond, aren't made of small molecules — every atom is joined by [[chem-covalent-bond|covalent bonds]] into one continuous 3D network. This makes them extremely hard with very high melting points.
chunks.checkText: A covalent network structure is held together by...

checkOptions.text: Covalent bonds linking every atom into one giant structure

chunks.heading: Diamond: every atom locked in
chunks.body: In diamond, each carbon atom forms a [[chem-covalent-bond|covalent bond]] to four other carbon atoms in a [[chem-vsepr-shape|tetrahedral]] arrangement. This makes diamond the hardest naturally occurring material.
chunks.checkText: In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?

chunks.heading: Graphite: strong layers, weak stacking
chunks.body: In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to only three others, forming flat layered [[chem-covalent-network-structure|networks]]. Weak forces between the layers let them slide apart easily, making graphite soft and slippery.
chunks.checkText: Graphite is soft and slippery because...

checkOptions.text: Its layers are held together by weak forces
Its carbon atoms aren't bonded to anything

chunks.heading: Sand's network structure
chunks.body: In silicon dioxide (the main compound in sand), each silicon atom bonds to four oxygen atoms in a [[chem-covalent-network-structure|network]]. Like diamond, this makes it hard with a very high melting point.
chunks.checkText: Silicon dioxide has a high melting point because...

checkOptions.text: Its atoms are linked by a network of strong covalent bonds
It has no bonds at all
